utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you questions related to trench digging and the death of these Muslims who were digging trenches at the front line. Did your son go to the front line during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which capacity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier. A soldier. Throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During his stay at the front line, was your son exposed to enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was 50 metres between the two lines, 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of his friends get killed at the front line during the war? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honours. It's irrelevant. Under the Geneva Convention and the rules of war, there are different rules for soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours, but a distinction should be made between trench digging as it is seen by the Prosecution and trench digging as presented by the Defence. It can be established very precisely in the Geneva Conventions, but it can also be defined like the way in which it is taken within the war obligation in terms of tasks that are carried out for the military. That is one subject. And then on the other hand, if somebody is intentionally exposed to trench digging, that could be a violation of the Geneva Conventions. I wanted to draw your attention to the danger involved of being at the front line -- involved in being at the front line, but perhaps we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, separate and apart from a legal debate on the applicability of the Geneva Conventions and so on and so forth, I just don't think that this particular question and comparison of what the witness's son was doing as a soldier versus those who were digging trenches as part of work obligation, I really don't think this is an appropriate line of questioning at this juncture. It seems to me it's more for legal argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully accept what Her Honour Judge Williams said. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a couple of questions which was -- well, the issue was raised during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are supposed to ask this witness before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, the topic which was in chief was not raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is not your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but there are some issues which is related to my client, and according to your instructions, if I well remember, you said that each Defence team can pose certain questions in redirect when it was -- it touches the interest of its particular client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, that was -- yes, before the Prosecution cross-examines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But it was not a matter during the chief examination. It was a matter during the examination -- cross-examination. And I remember that you said that we shall be allowed, the other Defence teams, if something which will be new, completely new in cross-examination, that we ought to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We have reviewed what happened before, what was said before. Counsel for other accused persons can put questions to the witness after examination-in-chief, before cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Right. If anything arises after cross-examination which may touch any of the accused, then those counsel who didn't call that particular witness may put questions to the witness before re-examination by the counsel who called the witness. In fairness to you, Mr. Pantelic, the Trial Chamber will allow you put the questions, but please follow the correct procedure the next time. Because it puts Mr. Lukic in a difficult situation, because this is a witness for his client, you see. So you may put your questions, and depending on whether anything arises, the Trial Chamber may allow Mr. Lukic to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do -- I'm grateful to the instruction of the Trial Chamber, and I don't believe because these are mostly political issues of SDS which was raised during the cross-examination, so I don't believe it will be -- but let's see. Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukovic, I am Defence counsel for Blagoje Simic. My name is Igor Pantelic. I'm just going to put a few questions to you. The Prosecutor asked you about what you knew about Biljana Plavsic, whether you knew that recently she admitted to having committing certain crimes. She did that before this Tribunal, but my question to you is the following: What is your perception of the war crime of persecution? Briefly, do you know about that? Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, that's clearly out of the bounds of what this witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, we are talking about Samac in 1992 and 1993. The Prosecutor asked you about some positions of the SDS. I am asking you the following now: In Samac in 1992 and 1993, to the best of your knowledge, the SDS, the local SDS, did they advocate in any way a policy of persecuting the non-Serb population in Samac? Do you have any such knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed that quite closely during those days before the war conflict, and I could not notice that, that there were such cases in the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also in relation to the Prosecutor's line of questioning, he asked you whether you were in favour -- or, rather, whether you were against the programme of the SDS that meant a division among peoples, partition, et cetera. Tell me, do you have any knowledge about whether the SDS ever in its political programme or officially espoused the idea of partitioning peoples along ethnic lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm not talking about territories now. I'm talking about the partitioning of peoples.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity of seeing the programme of the SDS, but I did not hear about that from the leadership of the SDS in Samac and in the territory of the municipality of Samac, that something like that was advocated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the same subject that was raised by the Prosecutor, that is the Prosecutor's own point of view, and they have the right to do that in relation to the position of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object to that. That's a speech Your Honour. He's talking about the Prosecutor's point of view and they have the right to do so. If he wants to ask a question, let him ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, do you know that in 1992 and 1993 the work of political parties in Republika Srpska was frozen? Do you know that? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last topic, because the Prosecutor asked you about that inter alia and you were responding to those questions, you were saying what you knew, of course, you said that whoever did -- went to the front line did not have work obligation, et cetera. Now I'm asking you the following: In 1992 and 1993 in Samac, as regards work obligation, were Serbs included in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Work obligation applied to the persons who made inventories of goods in shops. So work obligation is not only to dig trenches or to do other things. We engaged everyone who could work and who were incapable of going out to fight a war with a rifle in their hands. Regardless of ethnicity, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to that, Mr. Vukovic, do you know whether members of the Serb people in Samac, within their work obligation, went to the front line to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. You are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, who have made it possible for me to speak about what I know and within the scope of my possibility, and I would like to thank you all and especially Miro Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to take the opportunity of this break. We noticed on the official transcript we got for the last days that there was the name of the protected witness in brackets. I don't know whether that is in keeping with regular procedure, but I remember that during the Prosecution case there was only a sign that was put there instead of the actual name of the protected witness. But in the official transcripts, I'm saying that the name and surname of the protected witness are up in the corner. I wish to draw your attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, I'm informed that the matter has been picked up, and it will be corrected. Good morning. Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. Can I start now? Can I start now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please give us your name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Mladen Borbeli.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you the following: Could you please pause for a few seconds before answering my question. Since you and I speak the same language, we understand each other, but we should not overlap each other. We need to facilitate the work of the interpreters. So could you please just pause for a few seconds. So when you hear my question, just pause for a few seconds before answering.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I was born in Prud by Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: 1932, on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, tell me, what was the ethnic background of your parents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Borbeli, since when has your family lived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: My ancestors, my grandparents, came from Italy in 1904.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me what kind of education you've had?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I've trained as a machine locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is a craft isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes that of a machine locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you complete your schooling?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, at the Mebos company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you work there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I worked there until 1988. And after that, I retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've been retired since 1988?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've been retired since then, since 1988; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and in which year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: In Sombor in 1952.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your military service, did you have a military assignment, a wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: It was at the Mebos company in the later period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your name erased from military records after awhile?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you a member of any political party in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Apologise. I asked the witness about the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when I asked you, I was referring to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe just repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of a political party in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No. In the former Yugoslavia, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the multi-party system was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, where do you live?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I live in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is your flat? In which street?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: It is in Pera Bosic street number 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who gave you this apartment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: It was given me from the work organisation in which I worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it made available to you for your use or was it your property?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I was given it for my use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then purchase it later?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you something about developments in Samac immediately prior to the outbreak of the war there. Did you notice in Samac, towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, that the relations between people had cooled? Did you notice any change in the behaviour of the people in Bosanski Samac? Can you describe that for us briefly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, before the war, perhaps a month before the war, one could already discern and notice that people were dividing along ethnic lines. The Muslims and Croats would be together. But I socialised with all of them, with all the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could any tension be felt in Samac, and had the relations between people deteriorated? Were there any conflicts from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, the tension was not very high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear or see anyone [Realtime transcript read in error "finance"] erect any barricades in Samac in spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I heard -- I heard that barricades had been put up the exit from Samac, and they were there -- were there in existence for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear who had erected those barricades?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: The Muslims had erected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have a correction to the transcript. That is page 56, line 12, my question was did you hear or see anyone erect any barricades in Samac in the spring of 1992, just a correction of that word. The witness has already replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear about any shooting in the city of Samac on which occasion any of your acquaintances were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what it was that you heard?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I heard that three people had been wounded in a luxury car, and these were acquaintances of mine. When I -- and then I went to the scene of that the next day, and I could see for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these people who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Excuse me. I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the people who got wounded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Mersad, Danilo and Cizman and Tota as they were known by their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mersad and Danilo, these are two persons? So Mersad is one person. Danilo is a second person, and Tota is a third person? Sir, are you aware of the fact that prior to the outbreak of the war in Samac on April 16 and 17, 1992, people moved away their families from Samac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes. People got their families away, also some ten to 15 days before the war, and they would go to Croatia. Buses would arrive from Doboj, and then they would be bused across the Sava River to Croatia. That was some ten to 15 days before the war started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did they -- was it the members of all ethnicities that took away their families or was this the practice of just one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No. This was the practice of all the ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, please tell me, do you know Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I've known him for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Miroslav Tadic did before the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: As far as I know, he worked for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I was asking about the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Oh, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So since the time you met him and -- what had he done?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: He worked in the mechanical engineering school as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war. After he worked at the secondary school, did he set up a private business or --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes. He had a store, and he also had a catering establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this catering establishment the As Cafe?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it Cafe AS the catering establishment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes it is the Cafe AS catering establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you frequent the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you go to As Cafe before the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, not very frequently before the war. And also during the war I would only drop by occasionally. And after the war, I went there much more frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in this period before the war, when you went to the As Cafe, who were the patrons of the cafe? Was it members of the just one ethnicity, or Samac citizens of all ethnicities came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Citizens from Samac came, villagers from the nearby surrounding villages also came. I knew some of the people. Some of them I didn't and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Croats and Serbs come to the cafe?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, they all did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, before the war, before the war hostilities broke out in Samac, had you heard about the existence of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that you heard? Was this the 4th Detachment? Is it a military unit? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: It is a Territorial Defence formation which was supposed to protect the citizens in the event of war, as far as I am knowledgeable on the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who the commander of this 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Radoslav Antic was the commander. And I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Simo Zaric was a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held there in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Miroslav Tadic belonged to the 4th Detachment or did you know at the time, rather?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know before the war where the headquarters of the 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: The headquarters was across the street from the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, to the best of your knowledge, if you are not certain of a fact, please feel free to say so. Say, "I'm not sure. I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, I'm now going to ask you a few questions about the events which took place in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Where were you that evening between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I was in my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the evening that evening did you notice anything or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I went out into the street and I noticed groups of people with arms, with weapons, younger people. So I looked at them, and I told them, "Throw those rifles away and go home, children." They just stared back at me standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I think these were youths. These were lads of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone amongst them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Dark had already fallen. These were youngsters. In fact, I did recognise one of them. He had worked for Bicic. I don't know his name, but he worked as a waiter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how this young man looked?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: He was a blonde lad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come and address this group of people while you were there? Did someone come up to them and then leave the place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: When I went back towards my flat, a man by the nickname of Ibela came by, and he was some sort of leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I went up to my flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later, after this event, did you hear any shooting?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go out from your flat that evening?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: When the shooting started? No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in your flat all evening or did you go out anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I remained in the flat all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next morning, did anyone come to your building, to your entrance or in front of your flat? Did any men come?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They came in the morning around 9.00. I went down and opened the door for them. They came in, and I could see that they were army personnel. They were in camouflage uniforms. They then started to climb upstairs, and they told me to tell all the tenants to line up by the door -- to be in front of their doors and to hold their identity cards in their hands, to produce them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they -- these men tell you why they had come to your building? What -- were they looking for something?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They came to look for weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they search all the flats?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They searched all the flats. And if the tenants of some flats were not at home, they would break down the door and would go into such flats and search them, scour the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they enter your flat?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you describe what happened? How did they behave? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, they behaved correctly, in my view. They asked me if I had weapons. I said: "No, I'm a pensioner. I don't need that." With the three of them was a lad whom I didn't know, and he said, "You don't have to go into the flat of this Mladja [phoen]." But I said anyway, "Please come in and have a look for yourselves." So one of them entered my flat and searched it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, in your building were the tenants there members of all ethnicities, of all ethnic groups, or of just one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: In my building there lived people belonging to all the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the flats searched?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: All the flats were searched? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just venture a suggestion. Mr. Krgovic has established that -- from this witness that a group of armed men came to the flat, and is now seeming to move into -- on to a different topic. What he hasn't established is who these men were, merely that they had camouflage uniforms and were armed. Furthermore, the witness seems to say that with the three of them there was one lad that he didn't know. Presumably, therefore, he knew the others. So if these people can be identified in the context of this case it's important because of the matters in the indictment. If this witness knows who these men were, whether they were locals or whether they came from else where, what ethnicity they were, for that evidence to be of value to you, you should know who the men were, beyond the fact that they had a gun and were in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't completed this topic, actually. I'll get to that. Perhaps I just went off on a tangent a bit, but I'll get back to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, these men who were there, which accent did they have and what did you infer on the basis of the way they spoke?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I noticed that they spoke with a Serbian accent, coming from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they wore camouflage uniforms. Were they masked? Did they have something on their heads?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They were masked with green and black paint on their faces, and they also wore berets. The beret was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man who addressed you did he also wear a camouflage uniform like the others?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: He had glasses, dark glasses so I could not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters did not hear the witness when he described the berets. Perhaps he talked of the colour. Just ask him to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, what was the colour of those berets if you remember? I heard you say black, but --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Black, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man who spoke to you, did he also wear a camouflage uniform, and was he masked like the rest were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: He was not masked, but he did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about his uniform? Was it also a camouflage uniform like the rest?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No. No. He had a blue jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before you leave that topic, even though the witness had said he didn't know who this lad was, could we find out whether he was a local lad or somebody from elsewhere. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours, please, related to the question Your Honour has just raised now. The witness did say that he was addressed by the name of Mladja, which I suspect might be the diminutive of this witness's first name and indicates some sort of knowledge of the person and that, with respect, goes side by side with Your Honour's question. If that could be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, this man who spoke to you, was he a local, a person from Samac? How did he speak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: He spoke Bosnian. He was not a Serb from Serbia proper. But I could not recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, tell me, these apartments that were broken into and that had been empty, were they all locked irrespective of ethnicity or was a selection made, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Apartments were barged into, all of them regardless. The apartments of all the people who were not at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Borbeli, do you know Maslic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Velimir Maslic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does Velimir Maslic live in your building?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Velimir Maslic lived in my building, underneath me, on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his apartment broken into?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me, on that day did you go out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, on the 18th of April, did you notice any vehicles in the street where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I noticed a vehicle by the building where I lived, a military vehicle. And there was a soldier up there with a helmet on his head. He was shouting. "Hand over your weapons. Nothing will happen to you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people did -- did people surrender their weapons? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I didn't see that, but I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day when you saw that vehicle, you live in the street of Pera Bosic. Did you see Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric by that vehicle or in the street that day?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, I'm going to move on to a new subject now. I'm going to ask you something about living conditions in Samac after the 17th of April. During those first few days after the war broke out, were bakeries working and food shops in general? And what about the bread and milk supply during those first few days, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: When the war broke out, bakeries and other productions were not operating for a few days, two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was shopping organised? How did you obtain bread and milk?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: A refrigerator truck came, and bread was distributed from the truck free of charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take that bread?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other food products? Did you see anything else? I mean, did you get anything else? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, yes. Milk was also given out and other products, other food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get eggs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Well, I got eggs from some acquaintances on the second day of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said awhile ago that you live in a building where people of different ethnic backgrounds live. Did all of your neighbours receive everything that you got, bread and milk, et cetera? Was there any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Everybody got it. Everybody put their names down and went they're to pick it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, Mr. Borbeli, during those first few days after the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, did you hear of any order that white ribbons had to be worn?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice when you went out into the street, then, that somebody wore white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I did notice. I noticed two citizens who had those white ribbons. But this did not last long, only for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic backgrounds of those two persons were, the ones you noticed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic. Are we going to find out where the ribbons were being worn, on which part of the body?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe this for us, Mr. Borbeli? How did these people wear these white ribbons, where?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: From their shoulder downwards. They were about 20 centimetres long and about two and a half centimetres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any soldiers also wearing white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Apparently I missed it unfortunately. Mr. Weiner saw it. Apparently, the witness made some gesture and indicated and perhaps that should be entered into the transcript so that -- or perhaps the witness can be asked again to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To indicate, yes, how these were worn. He can even stand up for everybody to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please show this to us on your own shoulder, how these ribbons were worn?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Here and then downwards. The length was 20 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how wide?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Two and a half to three centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness showed his right shoulder and that the ribbon was worn on the top of the right shoulder and then down along the upper arm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where were they pinned, these white ribbons, at the top or the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They were pinned at the top, at the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, I'm going to ask you something. You were born before the war; is that right? I mean the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If I could interject at this point before we leave this point of white ribbons. Mr. Krgovic asked the witness a question: "Did you notice any soldiers also wearing white ribbons." And the witness said yes, yes he did. What remains unclear from that, therefore, is whether the people he did see wearing the white ribbons were in fact civilians or at least it implies that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Do you follow -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. He can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you: These two persons you saw wearing white ribbons, were they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Borbeli, did you wear these white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody order you to wear a white ribbon?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other civilians who, like you, did not wear white ribbons? Were there other such people?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, there were other such people, but this was only for a short while, only two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers you saw, how did they wear the white ribbons, the same way you described it just now or was it different the way they wore them? Did they also wear them here on their epaulettes or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Only here on the shoulder, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These ribbons that you saw that the civilians had, they were not armbands going around the left arm, for example?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were born before the Second World War; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that there were Jews in Samac before the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that these fellow citizens of yours, when the Germans took the town, were forced to clean the streets and wear wide yellow armbands around their arms?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Yes, I did see those yellow bands on the shoulder -- I mean, no, not on the shoulder, on the arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These ribbons that you saw these civilians wearing, did they look like the armbands that the Jews wore before the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, I'm going to ask you this: These first few days, did shelling start, and if so, when did the shelling of Samac start?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: Immediately. The shelling started immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you notice anything in town? Were people leaving Samac during those days after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: People were leaving Samac and going wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that in the streets, that the town was getting emptier?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: At first you couldn't really notice it but later on one could notice it. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please if I may be of assistance to the Chamber. The witness says people were leaving Samac in the initial days after the attack. For that evidence to be of benefit to you or the Defence or the Prosecution, you've got to know of it was all people, members of all three ethnicities or whether it was a certain group. Otherwise it doesn't really assist either the Defence or the Prosecution or the Chamber. So that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague for his assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, these people who were leaving Samac, what was their ethnic background? Did they belong only to one ethnic group or --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: All three ethnic groups. People were leaving Samac, people from all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your neighbours, these people who were leaving town, did they tell you why they were leaving Samac?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: They didn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I think out of fear, because of the shelling and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the time has come for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and continue at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borbeli, if you hear me, the protection -- witness protection unit told me that you are not feeling very well. If you are not able to continue, please feel free to say so. Or if you should at any time feel that you are too tired or that your concentration is declining, please tell us so and we shall, of course, see to it that the Trial Chamber takes an appropriate decision given your age and condition.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BORBELI
utterances.text: I think that I'm unable to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krgovic, maybe a longer break?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, I will have a lot of other questions too for this witness, and since I worked with him for quite some time during these days, I know him by now. He has already complained of his health condition, and I believe knowing the witness, that it would be better for him to continue on Monday, because by that time he would have sufficiently recovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Trial Chamber is of the view that the witness can stand down, and we can proceed with him on Monday when he's able to. Is there another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this moment. The next witness will be arriving tomorrow morning, and we will be ready to start with a new witness on Monday morning. Should any further complications arise in the health condition of this witness, but any case, we will have a witness ready for Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Next week it's afternoons. Yes, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just while we're on this very topic, I wonder if the Defence could indicate the order of the next two witnesses that they expect, two or three, if they have -- make sure there's no changes and so that we can -- the Prosecution can make its own plans for the coming witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The Defence of Miroslav Tadic has submitted a draft schedule of witnesses, and for the time being, we have no changes whatsoever. So the next witness is the witness with initials DW1/3, to be followed by Svetozar Vasovic, and after him Dario Radic. The only problem, but then we have been promised by the witness protection unit that this will be addressed, the Dario -- Dario Radic was only subsequently included on the viva voce list of witnesses because he did not have a passport. We found out in the meantime he's been issued with a passport but now he's had a problem with the visa, but we found out he will be able to present himself here next week. At any rate, if it is all right, we wish him to be interrogated last of these witnesses unless this problem is solved before that, in which case he will be the first one that week. We still have the two witnesses who should testify via videolink. Of course the Trial Chamber is aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I do apologise, Your Honour. Maybe it was escaped from my memory, but I think that according to the scheduling -- trial schedules that we have two consecutive weeks of morning sessions. So maybe -- is it appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You should always watch the court calendar as it comes out, because there are so many trials now. So just watch the court calendar as it comes out. We will adjourn now and continue our proceedings on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of January, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.00 p.m.,
